progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From Year 11: xylem carries water up from the roots; leaves exchange gases; diffusion (particles spread from higher to lower concentration) and osmosis (water moves across a membrane towards the more concentrated solution); photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide. From b01: the five-part loop, negative feedback opposes a change, and a single organ can be both receptor and control centre (the pancreas). Not assumed: stoma, transpiration, guard cell, turgid, flaccid, ABA, wilting, xerophyte, cuticle, sunken stomata.
progression.startsWith: Follow water loss through stomata. The video opens: On a hot, dry, windy afternoon, a plant in a pot can lose water from its leaves faster than its roots can take it up.
progression.stopsAfter: tracing water from the roots through xylem to the leaf, where it evaporates from cell walls into air spaces and diffuses as vapour out through stomata (transpiration), faster in hot, dry, windy air because the outside air is drier and wind removes the humid layer at the leaf surface; explaining why stomata cannot simply stay shut (the same pores let in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis); explaining how guard cells open a stoma (they take in potassium ions, water follows by osmosis, the cells swell, and the thicker inner walls make them bow apart) and how ABA closes it under water stress (potassium ions leave, water follows by osmosis, the guard cells go limp and straighten); building the plant's negative feedback loop (falling water content, root and leaf cells, ABA, guard cells, less water loss); explaining the cost of closing (less carbon dioxide, slower photosynthesis and growth) and wilting when loss still outruns uptake; explaining how xerophyte features save water (waxy cuticle as a barrier; sunken, hairy stomata trap humid air so diffusion slows; rolled spinifex leaves; small leaves; hanging eucalypt leaves stay cooler); comparing a response that switches on and off with built-in features that work all the time.
progression.nextLesson: practise feedback loop questions across the homeostasis topic (bio-m8-g03, route review change 7), then investigate plant water loss (bio-m8-p02).

teaching.task: A plant on a hot, dry, windy afternoon can lose water faster than its roots take it up, and it has no brain, nerves or blood. How does it keep enough water?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why water leaves a leaf (evaporation inside, diffusion out down a concentration difference; 2); why hot, dry, windy air speeds it (drier air, humid layer removed; 2); why stomata cannot simply stay shut (shared pore; 3); why guard cells open (ions in, water follows, thick inner walls make them bow; 4); why ABA closes them (ions out, water follows; 5); why the response is negative feedback (it opposes the fall; 6); why closing costs growth (less CO₂; 7); why each xerophyte feature saves water (barrier, smaller vapour difference, less surface, cooler leaf; 8, 9). Attention: a plant with no brain still responds within minutes (1); a deal with a price (3). Visual medium: one leaf window that the camera moves through, a matched stoma pair that opens and closes on the spoken cause, a leaf that turns into a xerophyte leaf, and a plant that wilts. Apply: interpret data (11a), explain and compare an unseen plant (11c). Remember: "ions move, water follows" and "waterproof, shrink, keep cool, trap humid air".
teaching.conversationalApproach: On a hot, dry, windy afternoon a potted plant can lose water faster than its roots take it up, and it has no brain, nerves or blood, yet within minutes its leaves can cut the loss, so the question is how a plant keeps enough water. Water rises in the xylem, evaporates inside the leaf and diffuses out through the stomata as transpiration, faster in hot, dry, windy air. The trade-off is that the same pores let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis. Guard cells open the pore by taking in potassium ions so water follows by osmosis and the turgid cells bow apart, like two long balloons taped along their inner edges. Under water stress, root and leaf cells make more ABA, which makes potassium ions leave the guard cells, water follows them out and the pore closes, so guard cells move ions, not water. The same five-part negative feedback loop fits, with no brain: the same cells detect and signal, the guard cells are the effectors and the response opposes the fall. Closing has a cost, less carbon dioxide and slower growth, and wilting follows if the soil stays dry. Xerophytes have built-in savings: a thick waxy cuticle and sunken, hairy stomata that trap humid air, and Australian examples (spinifex rolled leaves, small leaves, vertical eucalypt leaves) are sorted by whether a feature waterproofs, shrinks, cools or traps humid air. ABA closure is a reversible response and xerophyte features are always there, then two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: On a hot, dry, windy afternoon, a plant in a pot can lose water from its leaves faster than its roots can take it up. It has no brain, no nerves and no blood. Yet within minutes, its leaves can cut that loss. So how does a plant keep enough water?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a is an interpret and explain item on a graph (leaf ABA and transpiration while a pot dries), so the stimulus, signal and response are read from data. 11c is an explain and compare item on an unseen xerophyte (the stop: compare ABA action and xerophyte adaptations). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s each): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the card as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ1-02 (p 56): "investigate the various mechanisms used by organisms to maintain their internal environment within tolerance limits, including:" with the listed example "mechanisms in plants that allow water balance to be maintained (ACSBL115)". Physiological mechanism (scenes 4 to 7), structural mechanisms (8, 9) and the comparison (10, attempt 2). "Within tolerance limits" is carried by scenes 6, 7 and 10. B8-IQ1-01 (construct and interpret negative feedback loops) is practised once in scene 6, as a transfer of b01's template to a plant, and drilled in g03.

design.visualSystem: One leaf window owns the frame from scene 2: the new leaf cross-section plate, large, with the camera (`Cam`) moving between the mesophyll air space and the stoma, never stretched. The new matched stoma pair (surface view, open and closed) carries scenes 4 and 5. A small coded water budget bar graph sits at the upper right from the hook ("water in: roots" against "water out: leaves", two bars that change height with the narration), so the balance being maintained is always visible. b01's loop ring takes the frame in scene 6. The matched potted plant pair (existing turgid plate, new wilted plate) opens and closes the story (1, 5, 7). No people, hands or faces. Coded elements are limited to the loop ring, the bar graph, the attempt graph, signal pulses, vapour wisps (b02's `EvapDots`), arrows, chips and tags. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
